name: Orthodontic extractions avoidance critique

card.summary: The view that removing healthy teeth for braces can flatten the face, which leads people chasing a fuller profile to look for non-extraction treatment.
card.note: Whether extraction is needed is an individual orthodontic judgement; the profile effect is debated among clinicians.

quick.overview:
Orthodontists sometimes remove healthy teeth, most often premolars, to make room for crowded teeth. A line of argument in looksmaxxing circles holds that this can pull the lips and midface back and leave a flatter profile, so people who care about facial projection look for treatment plans that avoid extractions.

The argument is about how to keep or improve forward facial support while straightening teeth. Orthodontists themselves discuss the question and generally say the outcome depends on the case, the amount of tooth movement and how the plan is designed.
quick.how: In practice people ask for a second opinion, request to hear whether a non-extraction plan (for example expansion or a different tooth-movement strategy) is feasible for their bite, and compare predicted profile changes with their orthodontist before starting treatment.
quick.risks: Non-extraction treatment is not suitable for every case, and severe crowding can leave teeth pushed forward if space is not created some other way. Extraction is a routine, well-established part of orthodontics, and the decision rests on an individual examination by a clinician.

lead: The orthodontic extractions avoidance critique is the position, common in looksmaxxing communities, that removing healthy teeth as part of braces treatment can reduce facial projection and give a flatter face, and that patients concerned about their profile should look for plans that keep all their teeth.

Orthodontic extraction is carried out to create space so that crowded teeth can be moved into alignment; premolars are the teeth most often removed for this purpose [1]. Proponents of avoidance point to the lip and midface support provided by the dental arch and say that retracting front teeth into the extraction space can reduce that support. How this plays out for an individual depends on the starting bite, the amount of retraction, and the surgeon's or orthodontist's plan, and orthodontists debate the question in the professional literature.

chain: Ask whether the plan needs extractions
Choose a plan that keeps arch and lip support
angle.text: People use the critique as a prompt to compare treatment options before braces, aiming to keep the forward support the teeth give the lips and lower face.

paras: Healthy teeth are sometimes extracted ahead of orthodontic treatment, mainly when crowding leaves too little room for the remaining teeth to be aligned; premolars are the most commonly extracted teeth for this purpose [1].

Advocates of extraction avoidance say that pulling teeth and closing the space can draw the lips back, narrow the dental arch and reduce the support of the lower face. Some link this to wider claims in the community about jaw and midface development and the appearance of the profile.

Orthodontic clinicians who favour extraction in selected cases respond that the effect on the profile varies by patient, that careful diagnosis can improve profiles with protrusive teeth, and that avoiding extraction in a crowded mouth can have its own aesthetic and periodontal consequences. The wider orthodontic literature on the subject includes studies with differing conclusions.

No studies found specific to the looksmaxxing framing of this critique. Orthodontic journals contain cephalometric studies comparing profile changes in extraction and non-extraction patients; their conclusions vary between studies.

lore.intro: The idea circulates in jaw- and midface-focused looksmaxxing discussion as a reason to seek non-extraction plans.

claims.believers: Proponents say that removing teeth lets the front teeth and lips retreat, reducing facial projection.
claims.experts: Orthodontists report that profile changes depend on the individual case and the planned tooth movement, and findings across studies are not uniform.
